stem: Oxygen enters the blood stream from the alveoli in the lungs and carbon dioxide leaves the bloodstream to enter the alveoli. Most of the oxygen is carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells to the body tissues.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Outline how oxygen enters the blood stream from an alveolus.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.stem:
Fig. 4.1 is an oxygen dissociation curve for adult haemoglobin. The curve shows the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen at the range of partial pressures found in the body.

The values for plotting the curve are obtained in the laboratory by bubbling oxygen at different partial pressures through a solution of haemoglobin at $37^\circ\text{C}$ and pH 7.4. At a different temperature or pH the measured values will change, resulting in a different oxygen dissociation curve.

{{figure:figure_4_1.png}}

Fig. 4.1 shows that the percentage saturation of haemoglobin changes at different partial pressures of oxygen.
parts.text:
Use Fig. 4.1 to calculate the difference in percentage saturation of haemoglobin at the lower partial pressure of oxygen of $2.7\text{kPa}$ compared to the higher partial pressure of $13.0\text{kPa}$.

Show your working.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Explain the advantage of having a difference in percentage saturation of haemoglobin at lower and higher partial pressures of oxygen.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem:
In a person with sickle cell anaemia, the ability of haemoglobin to transport oxygen and carbon dioxide is severely affected.

The cause of this disease is a mutation in the gene coding for the $\beta$-globin polypeptide of haemoglobin.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Outline the differences between the $Hb^A$ (normal) and $Hb^S$ (sickle cell) alleles of the gene coding for the $\beta$-globin polypeptide **and** explain how these differences lead to a change in the haemoglobin molecule formed.
